design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study of the dopamine transporter (DAT) ligand [11C]WIN-35,428 in 6 abstinent people who had used methamphetamine, 4 abstinent people who had used methcathinone, 10 non-using controls and 3 untreated early Parkinson's disease patients. One scan per person; outcome is the binding potential k3/k4 from a three-compartment model with arterial input, in caudate and putamen. No cognitive or psychiatric testing; the neurological examination is reported only in one summary sentence.
can_establish: That this very small group of former methamphetamine users (and a group of former methcathinone users) had lower mean striatal [11C]WIN-35,428 binding potential than this control group at a single time point.
cannot_establish: Whether methamphetamine caused the lower binding (no pre-use scan, three different recruitment sources, other drug use and smoking not measured), whether it reflects loss of terminals rather than transporter down-regulation or a change in affinity (the authors accept a neuroadaptive process is possible), whether it persists or recovers (one scan per person), or whether it raises the risk of parkinsonism (no follow-up).

sample.recruitment: Methamphetamine users from drug rehabilitation treatment groups; methcathinone users identified through the US Drug Enforcement Administration while incarcerated on drug-related charges (the Discussion describes them as members of methcathinone distribution rings); controls from a university normal-volunteer office; newly diagnosed, untreated Parkinson's disease patients (Hoehn and Yahr stage II) from an outpatient neurology clinic (Materials and Methods › Subjects; Discussion, 5th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Users had to name methamphetamine or methcathinone as their drug of choice and greatest use. All participants were in good general health by history, physical examination, ECG, blood and urine chemistries, blood count, liver and thyroid tests, hepatitis and HIV screens; none took neuroleptics, methylphenidate or other therapeutic drugs at scanning; all agreed to avoid illicit drugs for at least 2 weeks and had blood and urine drug screens before PET. No minimum amount, frequency or duration of use is stated, and no psychiatric or head-injury exclusion is described (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.demographics: Controls: mean age 30.5 (SD 10.0, range 18–48), 4 men and 6 women. Methamphetamine: 37.5 (SD 8.1, range 26–45), 3 and 3. Methcathinone: 31.2 (SD 5.6, range 26–39), 2 and 2. Parkinson's disease: 53.3 (SD 10.4, range 45–65), 2 and 1. Only the Parkinson's group differed significantly in age, F(3,19)=5.3, p=0.008 (Table 1; Results › Demographics). Education, IQ, ethnicity, smoking and psychiatric history are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single scan). The number screened or excluded is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Each group came from a different source: treatment groups (methamphetamine), prison through law enforcement (methcathinone), a university volunteer office (controls). The user groups are tiny (6 and 4). All users were polydrug users, whereas controls had no history of drug abuse or dependence. The methcathinone users were drug manufacturers or distributors identified by law enforcement, an unusual group whose findings may not generalize.

exposure.measurement: Retrospective self-report from a telephone interview, a study questionnaire (number of uses, typical dose, frequency, last use, highest dose) and the drug-history section of the Addiction Severity Index; recent use excluded by enzyme immunoassay of blood and urine before PET (Materials and Methods › Drug use history; Drug screens). The authors concede drug histories and purity cannot be verified, but assert methcathinone purity was certain because the users made it (Discussion, 5th paragraph); this is an assertion, not a measurement.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, per person (Table 2). Methamphetamine (n=6): usual amount ¼ g/day (3 people), ¼–½ g/day (2) or 3½ g/day (1); largest single-day amount from ½ g to 8 g; duration of use 3, 3, 10, 12, 20 and 18–20 years; all six snorted, three also smoked and two also injected. Methcathinone (n=4): usual amount 1 to 3½ g/day; duration 2–3 years; oral and/or snorted. Frequency of use and lifetime amount are not tabulated.
exposure.polysubstance: All users had also used cannabis, LSD, benzodiazepines, cocaine and alcohol; amounts and frequency of these drugs were not reported or analysed (Materials and Methods › Subjects). Tobacco is not mentioned for any group. The authors argue that none of these drugs is known to cause lasting DAT changes (Discussion, 5th paragraph), although the same Discussion cites reports of cocaine-related DAT changes (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Negative blood and urine screens before PET (these detect only recent use); agreement to abstain for at least 2 weeks. From the last-use and scan dates in Table 2 (editors' calculation, month precision), the methamphetamine users had last used about 4, 5, 40, 42, 45 and 65 months before PET (mean about 34 months), and the methcathinone users 27–41 months before (mean about 35 months). The methcathinone users had been identified while incarcerated.

comparison.controls: 10 volunteers from a university normal-volunteer office with no history of drug abuse or dependence; 3 untreated early Parkinson's disease patients served as a disease reference group (Materials and Methods › Subjects; Results › Drug use).
comparison.matching: Not individually matched. Sex ratios similar; methamphetamine users were on average 7 years older than controls (not significant). Age was handled by ANCOVA and, separately, by a fixed correction of 0.8% DAT decline per year taken from a published SPECT study (Table 3 legend). Education, IQ, socioeconomic status and smoking were not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use DAT measure; no estimate of premorbid ability; psychiatric history not described; family history of parkinsonism not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: History of drug abuse or dependence excluded; controls' alcohol, tobacco and occasional drug use not reported.

outcomes.instruments: PET (GE 4096Plus) after about 20 mCi intravenous [11C]WIN-35,428; 50 frames over 90 minutes; metabolite-corrected arterial input; caudate, putamen and cerebellum regions drawn on MRI-coregistered images; three-compartment model with K1/k2 constrained to the cerebellum value; outcome k3/k4, called binding potential (BP) (Materials and Methods › PET scans). Neurological examination by a neurologist experienced with movement disorders (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
outcomes.validity_norms: BP reflects both the number of transporters (Bmax) and their affinity (Kd); the authors argue from Parkinson's and animal data that Kd is unchanged but did not measure it (Discussion, 5th paragraph). The neurological examination is reported without a rating scale or scores.
outcomes.operationalization: Reduced DAT density was defined as a lower group-mean k3/k4 than controls. Absence of parkinsonism rests on the neurologist's examination, with no data shown. No cognitive or psychiatric outcome was measured, although the summary paragraph says the decreases were not associated with overt neurological or psychiatric illness.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Two regions, each analysed two ways (ANCOVA with age as covariate; ANOVA on age-corrected values), with Duncan's multiple range test for post hoc group contrasts. Duncan's test is a liberal procedure; there is no correction across regions or analysis strategies (Materials and Methods › Data analysis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Regions of interest were outlined by an investigator unaware of participants' histories (Materials and Methods › PET scans). Blinding of the neurological examiner is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: BP (k3/k4), mean (SD), Table 3. Caudate: controls 7.5 (1.7), methamphetamine 5.8 (1.0), methcathinone 5.7 (0.9), Parkinson's 4.0 (0.9). Putamen: 7.3 (1.4), 5.5 (0.9), 6.1 (0.4), 2.3 (0.4). Printed percent differences from controls: methamphetamine −23% caudate and −25% putamen; methcathinone −24% and −16%; Parkinson's −47% and −68% (Abstract). Age-corrected values: caudate 8.7 (1.6) in controls vs 7.0 (1.2) methamphetamine and 6.7 (1.3) methcathinone; putamen 8.3 (1.4) vs 6.7 (0.9) and 7.1 (0.6), the methcathinone putamen difference no longer significant. ANCOVA: caudate F(3,18)=4.97, printed p=0.039; putamen F(3,18)=5.53, p=0.007 (Results › Caudate nucleus; Putamen). Editors' calculation (Hedges' g from the Table 3 means and SDs with pooled SD; approximate 95% CI from the large-sample standard error): methamphetamine vs controls, caudate g=1.08 (0.00 to 2.16), putamen g=1.37 (0.25 to 2.48); methcathinone vs controls, caudate g=1.09 (−0.13 to 2.32), putamen g=0.91 (−0.29 to 2.12). Simple two-group pooled-variance t-tests from the same table (editors' calculation, not age-adjusted) give p≈0.044 and p≈0.014 for the methamphetamine comparisons and p≈0.072 and p≈0.125 for the methcathinone comparisons, so significance of the methcathinone contrasts depends on the four-group error term and Duncan's test. Individual values are not shown; assuming normality, about 16% (caudate) and 10% (putamen) of controls would be expected to fall below the methamphetamine group mean (editors' calculation), so the distributions probably overlap.
analysis.covariates: Age only (ANCOVA covariate, or a fixed 0.8%/year correction that the authors say may be somewhat high). No adjustment for sex, smoking, other drug use or education.
analysis.selective_reporting: Individual BP values are not shown (Figure 1 shows one image per group), so the overlap between groups cannot be inspected. The neurological examination is summarized without data. No relation of BP to amount, duration or time since last use is reported, although per-person data exist in Table 2.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 6 users and 10 controls the 95% interval for the standardized difference runs from about 0 to above 2 (editors' calculation), so the size of the difference is very uncertain.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 6 former methamphetamine users and 4 former methcathinone users, mean striatal binding potential for a DAT ligand was 16–25% lower than in 10 controls, with a very imprecise effect size, no individual data, a single scan per person and unmeasured confounders (other drugs, tobacco, education). Three older Parkinson's patients had larger reductions, especially in the putamen.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract describe reduced DAT density and persistent reductions, and the abstract raises the possibility of increased risk of parkinsonism as users age (Abstract). Persistence is inferred from one scan after self-reported abstinence, and two of the six methamphetamine users had stopped only 4–5 months before scanning (Table 2). The Discussion weighs neuroadaptation against neurotoxicity and states the authors "tend to favor the view that DA neurotoxicity may be involved", on the strength of animal studies and the resemblance to Parkinson's disease, while conceding a neuroadaptive process is conceivable (Discussion, 2nd paragraph and summary). The Parkinson's comparison uses 3 patients about 20 years older. The summary says the decreases were not associated with overt psychiatric illness, but no psychiatric assessment is described in the Methods.

timeline.event: Post-mortem striatum of chronic methamphetamine users (Wilson et al., 1996, as described in this paper's Discussion): DAT and other dopamine markers reduced but dopa decarboxylase and the vesicular monoamine transporter normal, read by those authors as no terminal loss; McCann et al. answer that these markers may miss milder injury.
Baboon study from the same group (Villemagne et al., 1998) used by the authors to support a neurotoxic reading of lower [11C]WIN-35,428 binding.

replication.where_it_stands: To be completed from the later papers read in this batch.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service grants DA05707, DA06275 (G.A.R.) and DA09482 (D.F.W.); National Institute of Mental Health Intramural Research Program (U.D.M.) (Footnotes).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the NIMH Intramural Research Program and Johns Hopkins (Nuclear Medicine; Neurology). The baboon neurotoxicity study on which the Discussion relies (Villemagne et al., 1998) lists McCann, Wong, Dannals and Ricaurte among its authors (reference list). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective PET with both DAT and a terminal marker less subject to regulation (VMAT2) in people before and after starting regular methamphetamine use and after sustained abstinence, with matched controls rescanned at the same intervals, measured tobacco and other drug use, and individual values reported; post-mortem confirmation of terminal integrity in the same kind of users.

domains.note: Adjusted for age only. Other drug use (including cocaine) and tobacco not measured; education, IQ and psychiatric history not reported; no pre-use DAT.
Retrospective self-report of amounts and dates; one methamphetamine user aged 29 reports 18–20 years of use (Table 2).
Treatment groups, incarcerated drug distributors and university volunteers; very small groups.
Time since last use ranged from about 4 months to over 5 years; methcathinone users were identified in prison; if binding changes with abstinence, the group mean depends on when people were scanned.
No missing outcome data apparent; screening numbers not reported.
Arterial-input kinetic modelling with blinded region drawing. That BP mixes transporter number and affinity is an interpretation issue, not a measurement bias.
Two analysis strategies with a liberal post hoc test; the caudate p-value does not match its F statistic; no individual data; neurological findings not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The PET measurement is careful and blinded, but six methamphetamine users from a treatment programme compared with university volunteers, with only age adjusted and other drug use and tobacco unmeasured, cannot attribute the lower binding to methamphetamine; the effect size is very imprecise and the significance of some contrasts depends on the post hoc procedure.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine users (n=6) had lower mean [11C]WIN-35,428 binding potential than controls (n=10): caudate 5.8 (SD 1.0) vs 7.5 (SD 1.7), 23% lower; putamen 5.5 (SD 0.9) vs 7.3 (SD 1.4), 25% lower; both significant by ANCOVA with age as covariate and Duncan's post hoc test.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Caudate nucleus and Putamen; Abstract

key_findings.finding: Methcathinone users (n=4): caudate 5.7 (SD 0.9), 24% lower; putamen 6.1 (SD 0.4), 16% lower; after age correction the putamen difference was no longer significant.

Untreated early Parkinson's patients (n=3, mean age 53): caudate 4.0 (SD 0.9), 47% lower; putamen 2.3 (SD 0.4), 68% lower. Putamen binding in Parkinson's was significantly lower than in both user groups; caudate binding did not differ significantly between Parkinson's patients and users.
Four-group ANCOVA (age covariate): caudate F(3,18)=4.97, printed p=0.039; putamen F(3,18)=5.53, p=0.007.
key_findings.note: For F(3,18)=4.97 the p-value is about 0.011 (editors' calculation), not 0.039; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: With a fixed age correction (0.8% per year), methamphetamine users remained lower: caudate 7.0 (SD 1.2) vs 8.7 (SD 1.6); putamen 6.7 (SD 0.9) vs 8.3 (SD 1.4), about 19–20% lower.

Editors' calculation from Table 3: standardized differences (Hedges' g) for methamphetamine vs controls of 1.08 (95% CI 0.00 to 2.16) in caudate and 1.37 (0.25 to 2.48) in putamen; for methcathinone 1.09 (−0.13 to 2.32) and 0.91 (−0.29 to 2.12).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with pooled SD; values printed to one decimal, so approximate.

key_findings.finding: Time since last use, from the dates in Table 2: methamphetamine users about 4, 5, 40, 42, 45 and 65 months (mean about 34); methcathinone users 27–41 months (mean about 35). Two of the six methamphetamine users had stopped only 4–5 months before PET.

Self-reported use (Table 2): four of six methamphetamine users reported usual amounts of ¼ to ½ g/day and one reported 3½ g/day; durations ranged from 3 to about 20 years; all snorted, some also smoked or injected. All users had also used cannabis, LSD, benzodiazepines, cocaine and alcohol, not quantified.
Neither user group showed clinical signs of parkinsonism on a neurologist's examination; no rating scale or scores are reported.
The authors state that the lower binding could reflect a neuroadaptive process rather than neurotoxicity, while favouring neurotoxicity on the basis of animal data and the Parkinson's comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: Caudate ANCOVA reported as F(3,18)=4.97 with p=0.039; with 3 and 18 degrees of freedom, F=4.97 corresponds to p≈0.011 (editors' calculation). The putamen F(3,18)=5.53, p=0.007 is consistent.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the F or the p is misprinted. The conclusion at p<0.05 is unchanged, but the exact strength of evidence is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say all users reported about 3 years of abstinence, but Table 2 dates show two methamphetamine users (subjects 1 and 6) last used about 4 and 5 months before PET. The abstract's average of about 3 years matches the mean (editors' calculation about 34 months).
reporting_issues.consequence: The words persistent and lasting rest partly on people abstinent only a few months.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists the methcathinone putamen decrease (−16%) as significant without noting that the age-corrected comparison was not significant (Table 3); a simple two-group t-test from the table gives p≈0.13 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The methcathinone putamen finding is fragile and depends on the analysis chosen.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives 30 and 37 as the mean ages of methamphetamine and control subjects respectively, the reverse of Table 1 (37.5 and 30.5). It also says age-related DAT decline does not occur between 30 and 37, while the paper's own correction assumes 0.8% per year from age 10 (about 5–6% over 7 years).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; Table 3 legend)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the age argument is less secure than the text suggests, though the age-corrected values still show lower binding.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists a 29-year-old methamphetamine user with 18–20 years of use, which implies use from about age 9–11; not commented on.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a data error or an atypical history; illustrates the unverified self-report.

reporting_issues.issue: Title and abstract call the outcome transporter density, but the measure is k3/k4 (binding potential), which depends on both Bmax and Kd; Kd was not measured.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Title; Materials and Methods › PET scans; Discussion, 5th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Lower BP is compatible with fewer transporters, lower affinity, or competition from endogenous dopamine.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary says the decreases were not associated with overt neurological or psychiatric illness, but no psychiatric assessment is described in the Methods and the neurological examination is reported without data.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, summary paragraph; Materials and Methods › Subjects)
reporting_issues.consequence: The absence of clinical consequences is asserted rather than shown.
